stem: The three main types of movements of ocean water are waves, tides, and:
solution: The three main types of movements of ocean water are: (1) waves (the up-and-down/oscillating motion of the surface water, caused mainly by wind); (2) tides (the periodic rise and fall of the sea level, caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun); and (3) currents (the continuous, directed flow of a mass of ocean water from one place to another, like a river in the sea). Together these describe how the ocean water is in constant motion. Understanding the three movements of ocean water (waves, tides, currents) is a fundamental prelims point. The three main movements of ocean water are waves, tides, and currents.

stem: The up-and-down (oscillating) motion of the surface of the ocean, caused mainly by the wind blowing over the water, produces:
solution: Waves are the up-and-down, oscillating (rising and falling) motion of the surface water of the ocean, caused mainly by the wind blowing across the water surface (the wind transfers its energy to the water). In a wave, the water itself does not travel forward across the ocean — it mostly moves up and down (in circles) in place, while it is the energy (the wave form) that moves forward. The size of waves depends on the wind's speed, duration, and the distance over which it blows (the fetch). Understanding that waves are wind-caused surface oscillations is a prelims point. Waves are the up-and-down motion of the ocean surface, caused mainly by wind.

stem: The highest part of a wave is called the crest, and the lowest part is called the:
solution: In a wave, the highest part (the top) is called the crest, and the lowest part (the bottom, between two crests) is called the trough. The vertical distance between the crest and the trough is the wave height, and the horizontal distance between two successive crests (or two successive troughs) is the wavelength. These are the basic parts/measurements of a wave. Understanding the crest and trough of a wave is a prelims point. The lowest part of a wave is the trough (the highest is the crest).

stem: The periodic rise and fall of the level of the sea water (roughly twice a day), caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and the Sun), is called:
solution: Tides are the periodic (regular) rise and fall of the level of the sea water, occurring usually twice a day at most places, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun) on the ocean waters (along with the effect of the Earth's rotation). When the sea level rises (the water advances up the shore), it is high tide; when it falls (the water retreats), it is low tide. Because the Moon is much closer to the Earth than the Sun, the Moon's gravitational pull is the dominant cause of tides. Understanding tides (periodic rise/fall of sea level, caused by the Moon and Sun) is a key prelims point. Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.

stem: The main cause of the tides is the gravitational pull of the __________ on the ocean waters.
options: Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun)
solution: The main cause of the tides is the gravitational pull of the Moon on the Earth's ocean waters (with the Sun also contributing, but less). Although the Sun is far more massive than the Moon, the Moon is very much closer to the Earth, so the Moon's tide-raising gravitational pull on the oceans is more than twice as strong as the Sun's. The Moon's pull draws the ocean water toward it, creating a bulge of water (high tide) on the side of the Earth facing the Moon (and another on the opposite side), while the Earth's rotation carries places through these bulges, giving the regular cycle of tides. Understanding that the Moon is the main cause of tides is a key prelims point. The Moon's gravitational pull (aided by the Sun's) is the main cause of the tides.

stem: The especially HIGH tides that occur at the times of the full moon and the new moon (when the Sun, Moon, and Earth are in a line, and their pulls combine) are called:
solution: Spring tides are the especially high (and correspondingly especially low) tides that occur at the times of the full moon and the new moon. At these times, the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth are roughly in a straight line (an alignment called 'syzygy'), so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and the Moon act together (combine/reinforce) in the same direction — producing an extra-strong pull on the oceans and hence higher-than-usual high tides (and lower low tides). (The name 'spring' has nothing to do with the season — it means the tide 'springs up' higher.) Spring tides occur twice a month (at full and new moon). Understanding spring tides (extra-high tides at full/new moon; Sun and Moon aligned) is a prelims point. Spring tides are the extra-high tides at full and new moon, when the Sun and Moon are aligned and their pulls combine.

stem: The relatively LOW (weaker) tides that occur when the Moon is in its first or last quarter (when the Sun and Moon are at right angles, and their pulls partly cancel) are called:
solution: Neap tides are the relatively low, weaker tides (the high tides are lower than usual, and the low tides are higher than usual — a smaller tidal range) that occur when the Moon is in its first quarter or third/last quarter (half moon). At these times, the Sun and the Moon are positioned at right angles (90°) to each other, as seen from the Earth, so their gravitational pulls act in different directions and partly cancel/oppose each other — producing a weaker net pull on the oceans and hence smaller (neap) tides. Neap tides also occur twice a month (at the two quarter phases of the Moon), alternating with the spring tides. Understanding neap tides (weaker tides at the quarter moon; Sun and Moon at right angles) is a prelims point. Neap tides are the weaker tides at the quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles and their pulls partly cancel.

stem: Ocean currents are best described as:
options: The up-and-down motion of surface water
The continuous, directed flow of a large mass of ocean water in a definite direction (like a river within the sea)
The periodic rise and fall of sea level
The dissolved salt in the sea
solution: Ocean currents are the continuous, directed (regular) flow of a large mass of ocean water in a definite direction — like a vast river flowing within the sea. Unlike waves (up-and-down surface motion) or tides (periodic rise and fall of level), currents involve the actual horizontal movement of huge quantities of water over great distances across the oceans. Ocean currents are caused mainly by the prevailing winds, and also by differences in water temperature, salinity, and density (and are deflected by the Coriolis force and guided by the shape of the coasts). Understanding ocean currents (steady flow of water like a river in the sea) is a prelims point. Ocean currents are the continuous, directed flow of a mass of ocean water, like a river within the sea.

stem: Ocean currents are broadly of two types based on their temperature: warm currents and __________ currents.
solution: Ocean currents are broadly of two types based on their temperature relative to the surrounding water: warm currents and cold currents. Warm currents carry warm water from the tropics (low latitudes) toward the poles/higher latitudes (e.g., the Gulf Stream), warming the coasts and air they pass; cold currents carry cold water from the higher latitudes (or from ocean depths, by upwelling) toward the tropics/lower latitudes (e.g., the Labrador Current, the Peru/Humboldt Current), cooling the coasts they pass. This warm/cold classification is important because of the currents' effects on coastal climate and on fisheries. Understanding the two types of currents (warm and cold) is a prelims point. Ocean currents are of two types: warm currents and cold currents.

stem: The most important factor that causes/drives the surface ocean currents is the:
solution: The most important factor that causes and drives the surface ocean currents is the prevailing winds — the planetary winds (like the trade winds and the westerlies) that blow steadily over the oceans. As these winds blow across the ocean surface, their friction drags the surface water along, setting it in motion in the direction of the wind, and so generating the great surface currents. (Other factors that influence currents include differences in temperature, salinity, and density of the water; the Coriolis force, which deflects them; and the shape of the coastlines and ocean basins, which guide them.) Understanding that prevailing winds are the main driver of surface currents is a prelims point. The prevailing winds are the most important factor driving the surface ocean currents.

stem: A famous WARM ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of North America and keeps north-western Europe warmer than expected is the:
solution: The Gulf Stream is a famous warm ocean current of the North Atlantic. It flows from the Gulf of Mexico, up along the eastern coast of the United States, and then across the Atlantic (as the North Atlantic Drift) toward north-western Europe. This warm current carries tropical warmth toward Europe, keeping the coasts of Britain and north-western Europe much warmer (and their ports ice-free in winter) than their high latitude would otherwise allow. The Gulf Stream is a classic example of a warm current with a strong moderating effect on climate. Understanding the Gulf Stream (warm current warming NW Europe) is a prelims point. The Gulf Stream is a warm current that flows up the east coast of North America and warms north-western Europe.

stem: A warm ocean current, on reaching a coast, tends to __________ the temperature of that coastal region.
solution: A warm ocean current, on reaching a coast, tends to raise (warm) the temperature of that coastal region and the air above it. The warm water heats the overlying air, and winds carry this warmth onto the nearby land, making the climate of the coast milder and warmer than it would otherwise be (for example, the warm North Atlantic Drift keeps north-western Europe warm; the warm currents keep ports ice-free). (Conversely, a cold current lowers the temperature of the coasts it washes.) Understanding that warm currents raise coastal temperatures is a prelims point. A warm ocean current raises (warms) the temperature of the coast it reaches.

stem: A cold ocean current, on reaching a coast, tends to __________ the temperature of that coastal region.
solution: A cold ocean current, on reaching a coast, tends to lower (cool) the temperature of that coastal region and the air above it. The cold water chills the overlying air, and this cooler air affects the adjacent land, making the coast cooler than it would otherwise be — and cold currents are often associated with fog and with dry (even desert) coasts (e.g., the cold Peru/Humboldt Current along the coast of Peru/Chile, and the cold Benguela Current along south-western Africa). (Conversely, a warm current raises coastal temperatures.) Understanding that cold currents lower coastal temperatures is a prelims point. A cold ocean current lowers (cools) the temperature of the coast it reaches.

stem: The world's richest fishing grounds are often found where a warm current and a cold current MEET, because:
options: The mixing of warm and cold waters brings up nutrients and creates ideal conditions for plankton and fish
solution: Some of the world's richest fishing grounds are found where a warm ocean current and a cold ocean current meet (mix). This is because the mixing of the warm and cold waters (and the associated upwelling) stirs up and brings nutrients to the surface, and creates conditions ideal for the growth of plankton (the base of the marine food chain), which in turn attracts large numbers of fish. Classic examples include the Grand Banks off Newfoundland (where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current) and the waters off Japan (where the warm Kuroshio meets the cold Oyashio). Understanding why fisheries flourish where warm and cold currents meet is a prelims point. The meeting of warm and cold currents creates rich fishing grounds by mixing nutrients and boosting plankton and fish.

stem: A tsunami is a very large, destructive ocean wave (or series of waves) caused mainly by:
options: Undersea earthquakes (and also submarine landslides or volcanic eruptions)
solution: A tsunami is a very large and destructive ocean wave, or series of waves, caused mainly by a sudden, violent disturbance of the sea floor — most commonly a strong undersea (submarine) earthquake, but also submarine landslides or volcanic eruptions. Such an event abruptly displaces a huge volume of water, generating waves that travel across the open ocean at very high speed (with low height in deep water) but that grow into enormous, devastating walls of water as they approach and reach shallow coastal areas, flooding the coast. (The word 'tsunami' is Japanese, meaning 'harbour wave'.) The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was a catastrophic example. (Note: tsunamis are NOT caused by tides or ordinary winds.) Understanding the cause of tsunamis (undersea earthquakes, etc.) is a prelims point. A tsunami is a giant destructive wave caused mainly by undersea earthquakes (or landslides/volcanic eruptions).

stem: The regular difference in height between the high tide and the low tide is called the tidal:
solution: The tidal range is the difference in the height (level) of the water between the high tide and the low tide at a place. It is greater during spring tides (when tides are strong) and smaller during neap tides (when tides are weak); it also varies from place to place depending on the shape of the coast and the sea floor (some places, like the Bay of Fundy in Canada, have exceptionally large tidal ranges). The tidal range is important for navigation, fishing, and for harnessing tidal energy. Understanding the tidal range (high-tide to low-tide height difference) is a prelims point. The tidal range is the difference in water height between high tide and low tide.

stem: Tides are useful to human beings in several ways, including:
options: Helping ships to enter/leave harbours, aiding fishing, cleaning the shore, and generating tidal (electrical) energy
solution: Tides are useful to human beings in several ways: the high tide helps ships to enter and leave harbours and ports safely (they can sail over shallow sandbars and up estuaries at high tide); tides aid fishing (fish come in with the tide) and help fishermen; tides help to clean the shores and harbours by washing away silt, sediment, and refuse (keeping harbours clear); and the energy of the rising and falling tides can be harnessed to generate electricity (tidal energy/tidal power) — a renewable source of energy. Tides also affect coastal ecosystems (like tidal flats and mangroves). Understanding the uses of tides is a prelims-relevant point. Tides help ships enter harbours, aid fishing, clean the shores, and can generate tidal electricity.

stem: The energy of the rising and falling tides can be harnessed to produce electricity. This renewable source is called:
solution: Tidal energy (tidal power) is the renewable energy harnessed from the movement of the tides — the regular rise and fall of the sea level, and the tidal currents. By building a barrage (dam) across a suitable bay or estuary with a large tidal range, the water that flows in and out with the tides can be made to turn turbines and generate electricity. Tidal energy is clean and renewable (the tides are inexhaustible and predictable). (Places with a very large tidal range, like the Gulf of Kutch and Gulf of Khambhat in India, and the Bay of Fundy in Canada, are suitable for tidal power.) Understanding tidal energy (electricity from the tides) is a prelims point. Tidal energy is the renewable electricity generated by harnessing the rise and fall of the tides.

stem: Ocean currents flowing along coasts strongly influence the climate of coastal lands. This shows that ocean currents help in the __________ of heat around the globe.
solution: Ocean currents strongly influence the climate of coastal lands (warm currents warming coasts, cold currents cooling them), which shows that ocean currents help in the redistribution (transfer) of heat around the globe. Warm currents carry heat from the warm tropics (which have a heat surplus) toward the colder higher latitudes (which have a heat deficit), while cold currents carry cold water back toward the tropics. In this way, ocean currents — along with the winds — transfer heat from the equator toward the poles, helping to balance the Earth's heat budget and to moderate the world's climates. Understanding that ocean currents redistribute heat globally is a prelims point. Ocean currents help redistribute heat around the globe, from the tropics toward the poles.

stem: Assertion (A): Spring tides are higher than normal tides. Reason (R): At full moon and new moon, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned, so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon combine. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that spring tides are higher than normal tides. And the reason is (R) that at the times of full moon and new moon, the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth are aligned in a straight line, so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and the Moon act together (combine/reinforce) in the same direction. This combined, stronger pull on the ocean water is exactly what produces the extra-high spring tides — so R correctly explains A. (At the quarter moons, the Sun and Moon are at right angles and their pulls partly cancel, giving the weaker neap tides.) Understanding this cause-effect (alignment → combined pull → spring tides) is a prelims point. Spring tides are higher because at full/new moon the aligned Sun and Moon combine their gravitational pulls.

stem: In a wave, the water particles themselves mainly:
options: Travel forward across the whole ocean with the wave
Move up and down (in small circles) in more or less the same place, while the wave energy moves forward
solution: In a wave, the water particles themselves do NOT travel forward across the ocean; they mainly move up and down (in small circular orbits) in more or less the same place, while it is the wave form and energy that moves forward across the water. You can see this when a floating object (like a cork or a boat) bobs up and down as a wave passes, rather than being carried along with it. So a wave transmits energy through the water, not the water itself. (Only near the shore, when a wave 'breaks', does the water actually surge forward.) Understanding that wave water moves in circles (up and down), not forward, is a prelims point. In a wave, the water moves up and down in place while the wave energy travels forward.

stem: The horizontal distance between two successive wave crests (or two successive troughs) is called the:
solution: The wavelength is the horizontal distance between two successive crests (the high points) of a wave, or equivalently between two successive troughs (the low points). It is one of the basic measurements of a wave. (Other wave measurements: the wave height is the vertical distance between a crest and a trough; the wave period is the time taken for two successive crests to pass a fixed point; and the fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows to generate the waves.) Understanding wavelength (distance between successive crests) is a prelims point. The wavelength is the horizontal distance between two successive wave crests (or troughs).

stem: The distance of open water over which the wind blows to generate waves (the greater it is, the bigger the waves) is called the:
solution: The fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows (unobstructed) to generate waves. The size (height) of waves depends on three things: the speed of the wind, the length of time the wind blows (its duration), and the fetch (the distance over which it blows) — the greater any of these, the larger the waves. A long fetch (like across a wide, open ocean) allows the wind to build up big waves, whereas a short fetch (like on a small lake) only produces small waves. Understanding fetch (the distance the wind blows over water) is a prelims point. The fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows to generate waves.

stem: When waves reach shallow water near the shore, they rise up, curl over, and collapse forward — this is called a:
solution: A breaker is what a wave becomes when it reaches shallow water near the shore: as the water becomes shallower, the base of the wave is slowed by friction with the sea bed while the top continues moving, so the wave rises up, becomes steeper, curls over, and finally collapses/tumbles forward — 'breaking' onto the beach as surf. This breaking is the point at which the water actually surges forward (up the beach). Breakers/surf are what surfers ride and what erode and shape the coast. Understanding the breaker (a wave breaking in shallow water) is a prelims point. A breaker is a wave that rises up and collapses forward as it reaches the shallow water near the shore.

stem: At most places on Earth, there are __________ high tides and __________ low tides in roughly a day (a semi-diurnal pattern).
solution: At most places on Earth, the tides follow a 'semi-diurnal' pattern — meaning there are two high tides and two low tides in roughly one day (about every 24 hours and 50 minutes). So high tide and low tide each occur about twice a day, roughly 12 hours (and 25 minutes) apart. This happens because the Earth's rotation carries each place through two tidal bulges (one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side) each day. (Some places have a 'diurnal' pattern — only one high and one low tide a day — due to local conditions.) Understanding the usual semi-diurnal tide pattern (two highs and two lows a day) is a prelims point. Most places have two high tides and two low tides each day (a semi-diurnal pattern).

stem: The warm ocean current that flows northward along the eastern coast of Japan in the North Pacific is the:
solution: The Kuroshio Current (also called the Japan Current) is the warm ocean current of the North Pacific that flows northward along the eastern coast of Japan (and toward the north-eastern Pacific). It is the Pacific counterpart of the Atlantic's Gulf Stream — a warm current that carries tropical warmth poleward, warming the coasts of Japan. (Off north-eastern Japan, the warm Kuroshio meets the cold Oyashio Current, creating rich fishing grounds.) Understanding the Kuroshio (warm current off Japan) is a prelims point. The Kuroshio is the warm current that flows north along the east coast of Japan.

stem: The cold ocean current that flows along the western coast of South America (off Peru and Chile) is the:
solution: The Peru Current (also called the Humboldt Current) is the cold ocean current that flows northward along the western coast of South America, off Peru and Chile. This cold current (which involves the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich deep water) makes the adjacent coast cool and dry (contributing to the Atacama Desert) and supports one of the world's richest fishing grounds (great numbers of anchovies) off Peru. (During an El Niño event, the cold Peru Current is disrupted by warm water, harming the fisheries.) Understanding the Peru/Humboldt Current (cold current off western South America) is a prelims point. The Peru (Humboldt) Current is the cold current flowing along the western coast of South America.

stem: The cold ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of Canada, meeting the warm Gulf Stream near Newfoundland (creating rich fishing grounds), is the:
solution: The Labrador Current is the cold ocean current that flows southward from the Arctic along the eastern coast of Canada (past Labrador and Newfoundland). Near Newfoundland, the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream; the mixing of these warm and cold waters (over the shallow Grand Banks) creates one of the world's richest fishing grounds — but also causes dense fog in the area (and, historically, the icebergs the Labrador Current carries south were a hazard, as in the Titanic disaster). Understanding the Labrador Current (cold current off eastern Canada) is a prelims point. The Labrador Current is the cold current flowing south along eastern Canada, meeting the Gulf Stream near Newfoundland.

stem: Cold ocean currents flowing along the western coasts of continents in the subtropics contribute to the formation of coastal __________ there.
solution: Cold ocean currents flowing along the western coasts of continents in the subtropics (around 20°–30° latitude) contribute to the formation of coastal deserts there. This is because the cold current cools the air just above it; this cool air is stable and does not readily rise or produce rain (and any moisture tends to condense as fog rather than fall as rain over the land) — so the adjacent coast is kept dry, helping to form deserts. Examples include the Atacama Desert (along the cold Peru Current in South America) and the Namib Desert (along the cold Benguela Current in south-western Africa). Understanding that cold currents help form coastal deserts is a prelims point. Cold currents along subtropical western coasts help form coastal deserts (like the Atacama and Namib).

stem: The rising up of cold, nutrient-rich water from the ocean depths to the surface (which supports abundant fish, as off the coast of Peru) is called:
solution: Upwelling is the rising up (welling up) of cold, deep ocean water toward the surface, usually along certain coasts where winds and currents push the surface water away and cold water rises to replace it. This upwelled deep water is rich in nutrients (nitrates, phosphates), which fertilise the surface waters and support a great abundance of plankton and hence fish — making upwelling zones (like the coast of Peru, along the cold Peru/Humboldt Current) among the world's richest fishing grounds. (The opposite process — surface water sinking — is called downwelling.) Understanding upwelling (cold, nutrient-rich water rising, supporting fisheries) is a prelims point. Upwelling is the rising of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, supporting rich fisheries.

stem: The large, circular systems of ocean currents that circulate around the ocean basins (clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern) are called:
solution: Gyres are the large, roughly circular systems of ocean surface currents that circulate around the major ocean basins. Driven by the prevailing winds and deflected by the Coriolis force (and guided by the continents), the gyres rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise (counter-clockwise) in the Southern Hemisphere. Each gyre is made up of several connected currents (for example, in the North Atlantic: the North Equatorial Current, the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic Drift, and the Canary Current together form a clockwise gyre). Understanding gyres (the great circular current systems; clockwise in N, anticlockwise in S) is a prelims point. Gyres are the large circular ocean-current systems — clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern.

stem: The deflection of ocean currents (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere) is caused by the:
options: Coriolis force (due to the Earth's rotation)
solution: The deflection of ocean currents — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere — is caused by the Coriolis force, which arises from the rotation of the Earth. Just as it deflects the winds, the Coriolis force deflects the moving ocean water from a straight path (rightward in the N, leftward in the S). This deflection is why the great current systems circulate as clockwise gyres in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise gyres in the Southern Hemisphere. Understanding that the Coriolis force deflects ocean currents is a prelims point. The Coriolis force (from the Earth's rotation) deflects ocean currents right in the N and left in the S.

stem: The cold ocean current that flows northward along the western coast of southern Africa (contributing to the Namib Desert) is the:
solution: The Benguela Current is the cold ocean current that flows northward along the western coast of southern Africa (off Namibia and South Africa's west coast). Being a cold current, it cools and dries the adjacent coast, contributing to the formation of the coastal Namib Desert, and it supports rich fisheries (through upwelling of nutrient-rich water). (On the eastern side of southern Africa, by contrast, flows the warm Agulhas Current.) Understanding the Benguela Current (cold current off south-western Africa) is a prelims point. The Benguela Current is the cold current flowing north along the western coast of southern Africa.

stem: The vast, cold current that flows all the way around Antarctica (driven by the strong westerly winds) is the West Wind Drift, also called the:
solution: The West Wind Drift, also called the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, is the vast, cold ocean current that flows all the way around the continent of Antarctica (from west to east), driven by the strong, unobstructed westerly winds of the Southern Ocean (the 'Roaring Forties' etc.). It is the largest ocean current in the world (moving an enormous volume of water) and, flowing right around Antarctica, it connects the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans. It isolates Antarctica thermally, keeping it very cold. Understanding the West Wind Drift / Antarctic Circumpolar Current is a prelims point. The West Wind Drift (Antarctic Circumpolar Current) is the cold current that flows right around Antarctica.

stem: A high tidal wave that rushes up a river or narrow estuary from the sea as the tide comes in is called a tidal:
solution: A tidal bore is a wall or surge of tidal water that rushes up a river or a narrow, funnel-shaped estuary from the sea as the tide comes in (rises). It occurs where a large incoming (flood) tide is funnelled into a narrowing, shallowing river mouth, forcing the water to pile up into a moving wave or wall that travels upstream against the river's flow. Tidal bores occur in certain rivers with large tidal ranges and suitable estuaries (for example, the Hooghly river in India, and the Severn in England). Understanding the tidal bore (a tidal surge up a river) is a prelims point. A tidal bore is a surge of tidal water that rushes up a river or estuary as the tide comes in.

stem: The rising tide (when the water advances up the shore, from low tide toward high tide) is called the __________ tide.
solution: The flood tide (or flow tide) is the rising tide — the period when the tidal water is advancing and rising up the shore, moving from low tide toward high tide. The opposite — the falling/retreating tide, when the water is going down from high tide toward low tide — is called the ebb tide. So the tide 'floods' in (rises) and then 'ebbs' out (falls), twice a day. Understanding the flood (rising) and ebb (falling) tides is a prelims point. The flood (flow) tide is the rising tide, advancing up the shore toward high tide.

stem: The falling tide (when the water retreats down the shore, from high tide toward low tide) is called the __________ tide.
solution: The ebb tide is the falling (retreating) tide — the period when the tidal water is going down and retreating from the shore, moving from high tide toward low tide. It is the opposite of the flood (flow) tide, which is the rising tide. So each tidal cycle has a flood (rising) phase and an ebb (falling) phase. Ships often use the ebb tide (and its outgoing currents) to help them sail out of harbours. Understanding the ebb (falling) tide is a prelims point. The ebb tide is the falling tide, when the water retreats toward low tide.

stem: The warm ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of South America is the:
solution: The Brazil Current is the warm ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of South America (off Brazil), as the western arm of the South Atlantic gyre. Being a warm current, it warms the eastern coast of South America. (This contrasts with the cold Peru/Humboldt Current on the western coast of South America.) Understanding the Brazil Current (warm current off eastern South America) is a prelims point. The Brazil Current is the warm current flowing south along the eastern coast of South America.

stem: The cold ocean current that flows southward along the western coast of North America (off California) is the:
solution: The California Current is the cold ocean current that flows southward along the western coast of North America (off California), as the eastern arm of the North Pacific gyre. Being a cold current, it cools the California coast (giving it cool water and frequent coastal fog, and contributing to its dry, Mediterranean-type summers). (This is the Pacific counterpart of the cold Canary Current in the North Atlantic.) Understanding the California Current (cold current off western North America) is a prelims point. The California Current is the cold current flowing south along the western coast of North America.

stem: Places with a very large tidal range are suitable for generating tidal power. In India, sites suitable for tidal energy include the Gulf of Kutch and the Gulf of __________ (Khambhat), in Gujarat.
solution: Places with a very large tidal range (a big difference between high and low tide) are suitable for generating tidal power (tidal energy). In India, the sites considered most suitable for tidal energy are along the coast of Gujarat — the Gulf of Kutch and the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) — which have large tidal ranges, and also the Sundarbans area in West Bengal. The large rise and fall of water at these places can be harnessed to drive turbines and generate electricity. Understanding India's potential tidal-power sites (Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat) is a prelims point. In India, the Gulf of Kutch and the Gulf of Khambhat (Gujarat) are suitable for generating tidal power.

stem: One of the largest tidal ranges in the world occurs at the Bay of __________ in Canada.
solution: The Bay of Fundy, on the Atlantic coast of Canada (between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick), has one of the largest (highest) tidal ranges in the world — the difference between high and low tide there can be well over 15 metres. This exceptional tidal range results from the bay's particular funnel shape and dimensions, which amplify the tides. Such large tidal ranges make places like the Bay of Fundy attractive for tidal-power generation. Understanding that the Bay of Fundy has the world's largest tidal range is a prelims point. The Bay of Fundy in Canada has one of the largest tidal ranges in the world.

stem: The warm current off the eastern coast of Africa (in the Indian Ocean, off Mozambique/south-eastern Africa) is the __________ Current.
solution: The Agulhas Current is the warm ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of southern Africa (off Mozambique and South Africa's east coast) in the Indian Ocean. Being a warm current, it warms the south-eastern African coast. (This contrasts with the cold Benguela Current on the western coast of southern Africa.) Understanding the Agulhas Current (warm current off eastern southern Africa) is a prelims point. The Agulhas Current is the warm current flowing along the eastern coast of southern Africa.

stem: The current in the northern Indian Ocean is unusual because it __________ with the seasons, reversing direction under the influence of the monsoon winds.
solution: The currents in the northern Indian Ocean are unusual because they change/reverse direction with the seasons, under the influence of the seasonally-reversing monsoon winds. In the northern Indian Ocean (bounded to the north by the Asian landmass), the surface currents flow in one direction during the south-west (summer) monsoon and reverse to flow in the opposite direction during the north-east (winter) monsoon — following the reversing monsoon winds that drive them. This seasonal reversal of currents is a special feature of the northern Indian Ocean (unlike the fairly steady gyres of the other oceans). Understanding the monsoon-driven seasonal reversal of Indian Ocean currents is a prelims point. The currents of the northern Indian Ocean reverse direction with the seasons, driven by the reversing monsoon winds.

stem: The cold current that flows southward along the western coast of North Africa/Europe (off the Canary Islands) is the __________ Current.
solution: The Canary Current is the cold ocean current that flows southward along the north-western coast of Africa (past the Canary Islands) and off south-western Europe, as the eastern arm of the North Atlantic gyre. Being a cold current, it cools the adjacent coast (contributing to the dryness of the western Sahara coast). (It is the Atlantic counterpart of the cold California Current in the North Pacific, and it completes the clockwise North Atlantic gyre together with the North Equatorial Current, the Gulf Stream, and the North Atlantic Drift.) Understanding the Canary Current (cold current off north-western Africa) is a prelims point. The Canary Current is the cold current flowing south along the north-western coast of Africa.

stem: Ocean currents are also caused by differences in the temperature and salinity (and hence density) of sea water; the resulting slow, deep circulation is called the __________ circulation.
solution: The thermohaline circulation is the slow, deep circulation of the oceans driven by differences in the temperature ('thermo') and salinity ('haline') of the sea water — and hence in its density. Cold, salty (dense) water sinks in certain regions (like the North Atlantic and around Antarctica) and flows slowly along the deep ocean floor, while warmer, lighter water rises elsewhere; this sets up a global 'conveyor belt' of deep currents that slowly circulates water through all the oceans. The thermohaline circulation (unlike the wind-driven surface currents) operates in the deep ocean and plays a key role in the long-term redistribution of heat and in the ocean's role in climate. Understanding thermohaline circulation (density-driven deep currents) is a prelims point. The thermohaline circulation is the deep ocean circulation driven by differences in temperature and salinity (density).

stem: Warm ocean currents generally bring __________ to the coasts they wash, while cold currents tend to make the coasts they wash dry.
options: Rainfall (moist, warm air that can give rain)
solution: Warm ocean currents generally bring rainfall to the coasts they wash: the warm water heats the air above it, making it warm and moist and able to rise and produce rain over the nearby land — so coasts washed by warm currents tend to be warm and wet. Cold ocean currents, by contrast, tend to make the coasts they wash dry: the cold water chills the overlying air, making it stable and unable to rise and rain (any moisture forms fog rather than rain) — so coasts washed by cold currents tend to be dry (even desert). This is why warm currents are associated with wetter coasts and cold currents with drier coasts. Understanding this effect of currents on coastal rainfall is a prelims point. Warm currents tend to bring rainfall to coasts, while cold currents tend to make coasts dry.

stem: The time taken for two successive wave crests to pass a fixed point is called the wave:
solution: The wave period is the time taken for two successive wave crests (or troughs) to pass a fixed point — that is, the time between one crest passing and the next crest passing. It is one of the basic measurements describing a wave (along with the wave height, the wavelength, and the wave frequency). The wave period is usually a few seconds for ordinary sea waves. Understanding the wave period (time between successive crests) is a prelims point. The wave period is the time taken for two successive crests to pass a fixed point.

stem: Assertion (A): Cold ocean currents are often associated with dry coasts and deserts. Reason (R): Cold water cools the air above it, making it stable so that it does not rise and produce rainfall over the adjacent land. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that cold ocean currents are often associated with dry coasts and coastal deserts (like the Atacama along the cold Peru Current, and the Namib along the cold Benguela Current). And the reason is (R) that the cold current cools the air just above it, making that air cold, dense, and stable — so it does not readily rise; and air that does not rise cannot cool further to form clouds and rain over the adjacent land (any moisture tends to condense as low fog rather than fall as rain). This is precisely why cold-current coasts are dry — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this cause-effect (cold current → stable air → no rain → dry coast) is a prelims point. Cold currents make coasts dry because they cool and stabilise the air, preventing it from rising to give rain.

stem: Steady, long, rolling waves that travel far from the storm area where they were generated (having a smooth, regular form) are called:
solution: Swell refers to the steady, long, smooth, regular waves that travel far away from the distant storm or windy area where they were originally generated. As waves move out of the area where the wind created them, they become more regular, rounded, and evenly spaced (losing their choppy, irregular character) — this smooth, rolling motion is the swell. Swell can travel across entire oceans, arriving as regular waves on distant shores even in calm weather. Understanding swell (regular waves travelling far from their source) is a prelims point. Swell is the steady, long, regular waves that travel far from the storm area where they were generated.

stem: The three main types of movements of ocean water are waves, tides and:
solution: The three main types of movements of ocean water are waves (up-and-down oscillation), tides (rise and fall due to gravity), and currents (large-scale horizontal flow of water).

stem: The periodic rise and fall of the level of the sea water, occurring roughly twice a day, is called:
solution: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of the level of the sea, occurring usually twice a day, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on the ocean water.

stem: The main cause of the tides is the gravitational pull of the:
solution: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun) on the ocean water, along with the effect of the Earth's rotation.

stem: The especially HIGH tides that occur at the times of the new moon and full moon are called:
solution: Spring tides are especially high tides that occur at the new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line and their gravitational pulls combine.

stem: The relatively LOW (weaker) tides that occur when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth are called:
solution: Neap tides are lower-than-average tides that occur at the first and third quarters of the Moon, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other relative to the Earth, so their gravitational pulls partly cancel out.

stem: Assertion (A): Spring tides are higher than normal tides. Reason (R): At the new and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth are aligned, so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon combine.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Spring tides are higher because at the new and full moon the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line, so the gravitational forces of the Sun and Moon add together, producing a stronger pull — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Cold ocean currents are often associated with good fishing grounds. Reason (R): Cold currents and upwelling bring nutrient-rich water to the surface, supporting abundant fish.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Cold currents and upwelling bring nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, supporting abundant plankton and fish, which is why they are associated with rich fishing grounds — R explains A.

stem: Ocean currents are broadly of two types, based on their temperature: warm currents and:
solution: Ocean currents are broadly classified into warm currents (which flow from lower to higher latitudes, carrying warm water) and cold currents (which flow from higher to lower latitudes, carrying cold water).

stem: The most important factor that drives the surface ocean currents is:
solution: The prevailing winds are the most important factor driving the surface ocean currents; the planetary winds set the surface water in motion, and the currents are then modified by the Coriolis force and the shape of the coasts.

stem: A famous WARM ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of North America is the:
solution: The Gulf Stream is a famous warm ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of North America and across the North Atlantic, warming the coasts of western Europe.

stem: The warm ocean current that keeps the coasts of north-western Europe milder than expected is the:
options: North Atlantic Drift (extension of the Gulf Stream)
solution: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the warm Gulf Stream, flows towards north-western Europe, keeping its coasts and ports milder and ice-free even in winter.

stem: The rising up of cold, nutrient-rich water from the ocean depths to the surface is called:
solution: Upwelling is the rising of cold, nutrient-rich water from the ocean depths to the surface, often along coasts where winds push surface water away; it supports rich fisheries.

stem: The large, circular systems of ocean currents that circulate around the ocean basins are called:
solution: Gyres are the large, circular systems of ocean currents that circulate around the major ocean basins, flowing clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

stem: A tsunami is a very large, destructive ocean wave caused mainly by:
options: An undersea earthquake (or volcanic eruption or landslide)
solution: A tsunami is a very large and destructive sea wave (or series of waves) caused mainly by an undersea earthquake, volcanic eruption or landslide that suddenly displaces a large volume of water.

stem: The energy of the rising and falling tides can be harnessed to generate:
solution: The energy of the tides (the regular rise and fall of the sea) can be harnessed at suitable coastal sites with a large tidal range to generate tidal electric power, a renewable source of energy.

stem: Places with a very large tidal range are suitable for:
solution: Places with a very large tidal range (a big difference between high and low tide) are suitable for generating tidal power, as the strong flow of water can drive turbines.

stem: One of the largest tidal ranges in the world occurs at the:
solution: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has one of the largest tidal ranges in the world, with the difference between high and low tide reaching over 15 metres.

stem: Warm ocean currents generally bring __________ to the coasts they flow past.
solution: Warm ocean currents generally bring warmth and moisture to the coasts they flow past, making the climate milder and often wetter, as the North Atlantic Drift does for western Europe.

stem: Cold ocean currents flowing along the western coasts of continents in the subtropics tend to produce:
options: Cool, dry conditions and coastal deserts
solution: Cold currents along the western coasts of continents in the subtropics (like the Benguela and Peru currents) produce cool, dry conditions and are associated with coastal deserts (such as the Namib and Atacama).

stem: Match the current with its type: (i) Gulf Stream (ii) Labrador current (iii) Benguela current — (a) cold (b) warm (c) cold:
solution: The Gulf Stream is a warm current, while the Labrador current and the Benguela current are cold currents.

stem: The world's richest fishing grounds are often found where:
options: Warm and cold currents meet (and where upwelling occurs)
solution: The world's richest fishing grounds are often found where warm and cold ocean currents meet, and where upwelling brings nutrients to the surface, supporting abundant plankton and fish, as off Newfoundland and Japan.

stem: The up-and-down (oscillating) motion of the surface of the ocean water is called:
solution: Waves are the up-and-down (oscillating) motion of the surface of the ocean water, caused mainly by the wind blowing over the sea surface.

stem: In an ocean wave, the water particles themselves mainly:
options: Move up and down in circles (the wave form moves, not the water)
solution: In an ocean wave, the water particles mainly move up and down in nearly circular paths; it is the wave form (energy) that travels forward across the surface, not the water itself moving along.

stem: The distance of open water over which the wind blows to form waves is called the:
solution: The fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows; the greater the fetch (and the stronger and longer the wind blows), the larger the waves that form.

stem: The deflection of ocean currents (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern) is caused by the:
solution: Ocean currents, like winds, are deflected by the Coriolis force resulting from the Earth's rotation — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere — which helps create the circular gyres.

stem: Ocean currents are also caused, besides winds, by differences in the __________ of sea water.
solution: Besides winds, ocean currents (especially deep currents) are caused by differences in the temperature and salinity of sea water, which create differences in density; denser water sinks and flows, driving the deep 'thermohaline' circulation.

stem: A high tidal wave that rushes up a river or narrow estuary as the tide comes in is called a:
solution: A tidal bore is a high wall of water that rushes up a river or narrow estuary as the incoming (rising) tide is funnelled into the narrowing channel, forming a moving wave.

stem: The current in the northern Indian Ocean is unusual because it:
options: Reverses direction with the seasonal monsoon winds
solution: The circulation of currents in the northern Indian Ocean is unusual because it changes direction with the seasonal reversal of the monsoon winds, flowing in different directions in summer and winter.

stem: At most places on Earth, there are __________ high tides and __________ low tides each day.
solution: At most places on Earth there are two high tides and two low tides each day (semi-diurnal tides), roughly every 12 hours 25 minutes.

stem: The rising tide, when the water advances up the shore, is called the:
solution: The flood tide is the rising tide, when the sea water advances and the level rises up the shore; the falling tide, when the water retreats, is the ebb tide.

stem: The falling tide, when the water retreats down the shore, is called the:
solution: The ebb tide is the falling tide, when the sea water retreats and the level falls down the shore, following the high (flood) tide.

stem: The difference in height between the high tide and the low tide is called the:
solution: The tidal range is the vertical difference in the height of the sea between high tide and low tide; a large tidal range is useful for generating tidal power.

stem: The horizontal distance between two successive wave crests is called the:
solution: The wavelength is the horizontal distance between two successive wave crests (or troughs); it is one of the basic measurements describing a wave.

stem: When waves reach shallow water near the shore, they rise up, become steep and eventually:
solution: As waves reach shallow water near the shore, the lower part of the wave is slowed by the sea bed, so the wave rises up, becomes steep, and finally topples over and breaks, forming surf (breakers).

stem: Ocean currents flowing along coasts strongly influence the __________ of those coastal regions.
solution: Ocean currents strongly influence the climate of the coastal regions they flow past: warm currents make coasts milder and wetter, while cold currents make them cooler and often drier.

stem: Steady, long, rolling waves that travel far from the storm area where they were generated are called:
solution: Swell consists of steady, long, rolling waves that have travelled a long distance away from the storm or wind area where they were generated, arriving at distant shores as regular, smooth waves.

stem: The cold current that flows southward along the western coast of North America is the:
solution: The California current is a cold ocean current that flows southward along the western coast of North America, cooling the coastal climate of California.

stem: The cold current that flows northward along the western coast of South America is the:
solution: The Peru (Humboldt) current is a cold ocean current that flows northward along the western coast of South America; it supports rich fisheries and is associated with the coastal Atacama Desert.

stem: The vast, cold current that flows all the way around Antarctica is the:
solution: The West Wind Drift, or Antarctic Circumpolar Current, is a vast, cold ocean current that flows all the way around Antarctica, driven by the strong westerly winds of the Southern Ocean.

stem: The warm current that flows northward along the eastern coast of Asia (off Japan) is the:
solution: The Kuroshio current is a warm ocean current that flows northward along the eastern coast of Asia, past Japan, warming its climate, similar to the role of the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic.

stem: The cold ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of Canada, past Newfoundland, is the:
solution: The Labrador current is a cold ocean current that flows southward along the eastern coast of Canada; where it meets the warm Gulf Stream off Newfoundland, it creates rich fishing grounds and fog.

stem: A cold ocean current, on reaching a coast, tends to __________ the temperature of that coast.
solution: A cold ocean current lowers the temperature of the coast it flows past, cooling the adjacent climate, in contrast to the warming effect of a warm current.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Movements of Ocean Water' is that:
options: Ocean water moves through waves, tides and currents, which greatly influence climate, life and human activities
solution: The chapter concludes that ocean water is in constant motion through waves (wind-driven oscillations), tides (gravitational rise and fall) and currents (large horizontal flows), and that these movements greatly influence the world's climate, marine life, fishing, navigation and energy resources.
